newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia hopes labour law will stop worker unrest.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia hopes labour law will stop worker unrest.

text.p: Cambodia's National Assembly on Friday passed a long-awaited labour law that parliamentarians said would address the increasingly tense labour unrest in the garment sector.

The United States has indicated that the legislation, which needs the signature of King Norodom Sihanouk to become law, is a prerequisite for Cambodia obtaining Generalised System of Preferences status, which lowers or eliminates trade tarrifs.

It is Cambodia's first legislation protecting workers' rights to strike and bargain collectively. The measures also provide for the setting of a minumum wage, a 48-hour work week, overtime pay, compensation for accidents and paid leave.
Passage of the law came as garment manufacturers gave warning of economic gridlock after a spate of demonstrations and strikes.

"If the rules (in Cambodia) cannot be effectively enforced, investments will fail, unemployment will be rampant, and (the) country cannot progress," the Garment Manufacturers' Association in Cambodia said in a statement.
Association chairman Van Sou Ieng told Reuters that nine protests in the past month, all led by opposition leader Sam Rainsy, had left a bad taste for foreign investors.
"The fact is, manufacturers will close down here. Three or four garment manufacturers are already intending to sell their machines," he said.
The garment industry has agreed to industry-wide concessions, but some strikes have continued. Van Sou Ieng said the unrest showed the situation had become politicised.
The government has taken increasingly tough measures against the protests, using fire hoses to spray demonstrators and removing Sam Rainsy from factory property.
On Thursday, police fired shots into the air at the Hong Kong-owned Tack Fat Garments Ltd factory to break up a small demonstration and swung punches at Sam Rainsy and his deputy.
Finance Minister Keat Chhon said the 387-article law was well-balanced.
"This law will help us solve (labour disputes) in a peaceful way...in a legal way and not transform it (into) a political tool," he said.
